hi, it would be interesting to be able to offer the user the choice of the directory, were it not for the fact that we also have to modify the "launcher", the "remove" script and the link in $PATH. I have decided to [use the /opt folder for the purpose it is intended](https://tldp.org/LDP/Linux-Filesystem-Hierarchy/html/opt.html) (LSB - Linux Standard Base).
Another advantage is that the applications (if installed at system level) are also available for other accounts (if there are multiple people using the same computer), and its this latter aspect which led me to write "AM".

PS: I have already created something that can install the programs locally, its name is "[AppMan](https://github.com/ivan-hc/AppMan)", but it was just my first experiment and it did not fully satisfy my concept of application manager. That's why I wrote "AM".

Yep I read your intention about creating this and do fully agree. Yet `/opt` is the location where other locally-compiled application already resides and may create a conflict. If you want to make the application available at system level, I suggest you to move the AM applications to install not directly to `/opt` folder, but either inside `/opt/am` or /`opt/AM`. Just my two cents. Cheers,

thank you for your interest, but I repeat that the apps are installed in /opt just as the LSB wants. For example, the Firefox installation scripts place the application just [as suggested in the Debian wiki](https://wiki.debian.org/Firefox#From_Mozilla_binaries), while Google Chrome is installed right in / opt (and only in /opt), [as it is already structured in the .deb package it is taken from](https://www.ubuntuupdates.org/package/google_chrome/stable/main/base/google-chrome-stable), the same is for [the OnlyOffice .deb package](https://github.com/ONLYOFFICE/DesktopEditors/releases/latest). So the choice is certainly not mine and mine alone, but LSB's. 

The only thing you could dispute is the choice of launchers in /usr/share/applications, while for binaries I preferred to force links in /usr/local/bin. These may overwrite existing installations of the same software, so [I have already warned users of this problem](https://github.com/ivan-hc/AM-application-manager#important), by advising them to choose only one version of the same software, either from "AM" or their package manager, but NEVER TOGETHER.

Finally, my goal is to provide official software from the original developer sites and / or repositories, so brave (for now AppImage), gimp, vlc, inkscape, chromium / chromium ungoogled (for now from Slackware), Vivaldi Stable ( for now from Arch Linux) are just some of the interim scripts that need to be rewritten, and that's my priority right now. Placing all these external and (in fact) "optional" (hence the name of the directory /opt) programs in that specific folder is certainly the right choice that someone could make for a third party package manager, without therefore having to add additional folders to the root, ie "/" ( unlike snappy, flatpak and the GNU/Linux distribution Nitrux, with its /Applications folder).

I've installed a VM of Debian 11 i686 right now and I can reproduce the same error messages.

Chromium only works with the `--no-sandbox` option. I had more problems with the old laptop.

In general, the problem is running any chromium-based browser on a 32bit architecture. The more is old the hardware, the more we will have troubles. 

From what I understand, Chromium expects to be able to take advantage of full hardware acceleration, but unable to find the necessary components, it crashes. I tried to disable hardware acceleration, but the problem still exists.

I need to see if the base system needs kernel headers or additional drivers.

Well, now the whole scenario is clear to me:

On [Arch Linux at 32bit the Chromium version is the same](https://archlinux32.org/packages/?q=chromium) as [Debian 11  32bit](https://packages.debian.org/bullseye/chromium), i.e. 90, while [in the Debian Unstable repositories the version is 93](https://packages.debian.org/sid/chromium), as the team is working to ensure the same version for all supported architectures . [Other distributions](https://repology.org/project/chromium/versions) have dropped support for the 32bit architecture, which is why they can afford to work on the newer versions (currently Chromium 96).
[As for Slackware, I think that the availability of the two packages in the repository](http://www.slackware.com/~alien/slackbuilds/chromium/pkg/current/) (at [the opening of this "issue"](https://github.com/ivan-hc/AM-application-manager/issues/4#issue-1088917663)) is due to the fact that the 32bit version 96 does not work well on Slackware, so the developer wanted to make the version also available 89 for 32bit Slackware Current, not 64bit Slackware Current.

So [the problem is definitely related to the compatibility between Chromium (and its derivatives) with the 32bit architecture for Linux](https://github.com/ivan-hc/AM-application-manager/issues/4#issuecomment-1001649883).

We can't appeal to none, as [Chromium is just an experimental developer version of Google Chrome](https://www.chromium.org/), and therefore no official build is released.
[Whoever distributes Chromium Stable is certainly an external developer](https://chromium.woolyss.com/), and does it for their own Linux distribution of origin, it is certainly not Google that guarantees its availability. The fact that there are no Google Chrome builds available for the 32bit architecture is another proof that I am right.

So if we want the latest Stable version of Chromium for 32bit architecture we have to rely on the one made available in our distribution's repositories for 32bit.

This version distributed by "AM" is actually the one from Slackware, so I will try to replace it with the previous one made available for Slackware, if you really want a 100% working version, and yo you want.

Otherwise we would have to build a 32-bit version by ourselves and that can fully support all the limitations of the 32-bit architecture today, at the end of 2021, ant as I've already said, this is not an easy task for anyone want to distribute the official Chromium Stable release.

Anyone who wants to use Chromium 96 on 32bit architecture today will not have an easy time, and if it really works, they will be forced to run it with the `--no-sandbox` option, for now.

I could not find other reasons, current browsers focus a lot on hardware acceleration to reproduce multimedia content that without compatible codecs they could never reproduce.

We can therefore consider this issue closed.

MPV is a small package that requires a lot of packages in the background, so the final AppImage is bigger than what we have in a normal installation from the repositories. As it is already warned, AppImages created with pkg2appimage may be bloated, see the documentation here https://docs.appimage.org/packaging-guide/converting-binary-packages/pkg2appimage.html and this is not the only case, a lot of AppImages are bigger than a normal installation with shared libraries (never bigger than Flatpak, but bigger if compared with the conterpart from APT/PAcMan/DNF/any distro's package manager). This is the problem with having all the dependencies dedicated. 
However, AppImage is a compressed format, so after compiling and exporting the AppImage, thi final result is little compared with the AppDir, for example, VLC takes 115 MB in AppImage (the AppDir is about 400 MB), GIMP 150 MB (AppDir is 450), 0ad is 1,7 GB (AppDir is 3,1 GB), etcetera etcetera... and all these programs are not officially provided as AppImages from their main sites, so  we have to compile them (with pkg2appimage) the same way we do from git with any compiler, for example to compile Chromium browser from source you need over 1GB of files before extracting the 280 MB of real browser, and this is the whole work of a developer on the background, before him shares the final package on a site or repository. 
Compiling takes time and data to be downloaded, and this is what happens before you get MPV, VLC or GIMP from "AM"/AppMan. It is so, at least until an official AppImage os standalone package is provided by their developers officially.

The icon's path each app installed has via AM is `/opt/$APP/icons`, so this is not a path recognized by the Linux standards (normally `/usr/share/icons` or `/usr/share/pixmaps`).

To fix this you should copy the launcher of each app to your `$HOME/.local/share/applications` (if it does not exists, just create it), then use your text editor and change the `Icon=/opt/$APP/icons/$APP` entry to  `Icon=$APP` or the name of the icon you want to see.

If you install `menulibre` you can change the icons and edit the launchers on the application's menu easily with a GUI app.

AM aims to use only original parts from each application it manages.

OK, I think I have solved, from now the version installed will be compared with the last update, copy paste the following new updater in your AM-updater script and made it executable
```
#!/usr/bin/env bash
APP=duckstation
REPO="stenzek/duckstation"
version0=$(cat /opt/$APP/version)
version=$(wget -q https://api.github.com/repos/$REPO/releases/latest -O - | grep -w -v i386 | grep -w -v i686 | grep -w -v arm64 | grep -w -v armv7l | grep browser_download_url | grep -i appimage | cut -d '"' -f 4 | head -1)
updatedat=$(wget -q https://api.github.com/repos/$REPO/releases/latest -O - | grep updated_at | cut -d '"' -f 4 | head -1)
if [ $updatedat = $version0 ]; then
  echo "Update not needed!"
else
  notify-send "A new version of $APP is available, please wait"
  mkdir /opt/$APP/tmp
  cd /opt/$APP/tmp
  wget $version
  if ls . | grep mage; then
	cd ..
  	if test -f ./tmp/*mage; then rm ./version
  	fi
  	echo $updatedat >> ./version
  	mv --backup=t ./tmp/*mage ./$APP
  	chmod a+x /opt/$APP/$APP
  	rm -R -f ./tmp ./*~
  fi
  notify-send "$APP is updated!"
fi

#!/bin/sh

# NAME OF THE APP BY REPLACING "SAMPLE"
APP=resources
BIN="$APP" #CHANGE THIS IF THE NAME OF THE BINARY IS DIFFERENT FROM "$APP" (for example, the binary of "obs-studio" is "obs")
DEPENDENCES="base-devel"
BASICSTUFF="binutils gzip"

# ADD A VERSION, THIS IS NEEDED FOR THE NAME OF THE FINEL APPIMAGE, IF NOT AVAILABLE ON THE REPO, THE VALUE COME FROM AUR, AND VICE VERSA
for REPO in { "core" "extra" "community" "multilib" }; do
echo "$(wget -q https://archlinux.org/packages/$REPO/x86_64/$APP/flag/ -O - | grep $APP | grep details | head -1 | grep -o -P '(?<=/a> ).*(?= )' | grep -o '^\S*')" >> version
done
VERSION=$(cat ./version | grep -w -v "" | head -1)
VERSIONAUR=$(wget -q https://aur.archlinux.org/cgit/aur.git/plain/PKGBUILD?h=$APP -O - | grep pkgver | head -1 | cut -c 8-)

# CREATE THE APPDIR (DON'T TOUCH THIS)...
wget -q https://github.com/AppImage/AppImageKit/releases/download/continuous/appimagetool-x86_64.AppImage -O appimagetool
chmod a+x appimagetool
mkdir $APP.AppDir

# ENTER THE APPDIR
cd $APP.AppDir

# SET APPDIR AS A TEMPORARY $HOME DIRECTORY, THIS WILL DO ALL WORK INTO THE APPDIR

sed -i "s#/usr/share/applications#/usr/local/share/applications#g" ./$arg
```
original lines are these:
```
										chmod a+x ./$arg
										sed -i "s#wget #wget -q --show-progress #g" ./$arg

they should look like this:

do this every time you update with options `-u` and `-s`.

## How to prevent AM updating itself
This step is needed to keep your custom /opt/am/APP-MANAGER file without updating it:
- find and remove `$AMCLIPATH -s` from the file (originally it is the line 1530, if you add the line above it become 1531), this will prevent `-u` of using the option `-s` to update the /opt/am/APP-MANAGER script;
- in addition, remove the option `-s` completelly, these lines:
```
  '-s'|'sync')
    	if [ -n "$SUDO_COMMAND" ]; then 
		echo -e "\n WARNING: You don't need to run the option '$1' with SUDO.\n"; 
		exit; 
	fi
	
  	rm -R -f $AMPATH/$arch-apps $AMPATH/list && wget -q $AMREPO/programs/$arch-apps -P $AMPATH && echo -e "$(cat $AMPATH/$arch-apps | awk -v FS="(◆ | : )" '{print $2}')" >> $AMPATH/list
	cd $AMPATH && cat options >> list
	echo ""; echo ' SYNCHRONIZING "'$(echo $AMCLI | tr a-z A-Z)'" VERSION '$($AMCLIPATH -v)'...'; sleep 0.5; echo "";
  	rm -R -f $AMPATH/.cache/* 1>/dev/null; cd $AMPATH/.cache; wget -q $AMREPO/APP-MANAGER && chmod a+x ./APP-MANAGER; cd ..;
  	mv $AMPATH/.cache/APP-MANAGER $AMPATH; chmod 777 $AMPATH; echo ' THE "'$(echo $AMCLI | tr a-z A-Z)'" SCRIPT IS NOW UPDATED TO THE '$($AMCLIPATH -v)' VERSION! '; echo ""
	;;
```

Now you have an "immutable" version of "AM" (immutable in the sense that new features will not be added anymore... at least until you download it again manually).

Nope, AppimageHub.com and AppImage.github.io are not repositories, they don't offer constant updates and an AppImage managing like this.

AM is a repository of installation scripts inspired to the AUR, it does not contain packages but a way to install them easily and keeps them always updated.

AM does not manages just AppImages, it also manages official releases of Firefox, Blender and other standalone apps.

And AM is already the richest of apps listed, among the three catalogues (more than 1700 apps listed are AppImages). AppImageHub.com have a limited number of apps if compared with AM, the most of them are also outdated, broken and insecure (NOTE, even among the apps managed by AM there are old and abandoned projects, but at least the source is clearly visible, and it is assumed that the user is aware of what he wants to install).

The frontend of the database of AM is https://portable-linux-apps.github.io, each page is open source and contains the links to the main sites of the developers and a preview of each installation script (so the user knows what that script will do on its PC while running it using AM).

AM is always updated, and also if I will die soon or later, each installation script will still continue working offering the latest version of each app and a way to downgrade them (if URLs and APIs will not change in the future). AM for me it's basically a kind of legacy to the open source world.

Finally, I don't like the way Pling services ask for donations to support users, I can understand the creation of pages and uploads by third-paty users, but these users are not always the original developers and end up making money off the work of others. I don't like this way of doing things at all.

This is based on am2pla-site, made it executable and wait until the apps.json fie is ready:

```
#!/usr/bin/env bash

# THIS SCRIPT IS NEEDED TO GENERATE A JSON FILE OF ALL APPLICATIONS WITH EASE
cd $(xdg-user-dir DESKTOP)
AMREPO="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ivan-hc/AM-application-manager/main"
arch="x86_64"
echo "" >> args
wget -q $AMREPO/programs/$arch-apps && echo -e "$(cat ./$arch-apps | awk -v FS="(◆ | : )" '{print $2}')" >> args
echo STOP >> args
ARGS=$(sed '1d' ./args)
echo "[" >> apps.json
# THIS IS THE WORKFLOW
for arg in $ARGS; do
	for var in $arg; do
	if [ $arg == STOP ]; then
		break
	else
	case $arg in
	am) ;;
	appman) ;;
	*) for var in $arg;
		do
		description=$(cat $arch-apps | grep "◆ $arg :" | sed 's/"//g' | sed 's/^.*: //')
		echo -e '  {\n    "packageName": "'$arg'",\n    "description": "'$description'..",\n    "icon": "https://portable-linux-apps.github.io/icons/'$arg'.png"\n  },' >> apps.json
		sleep 0.005
		done;;
	esac
	fi
done
done
sed -i '$s/,$//' apps.json
echo -e "]" >> apps.json
rm ./args ./$arch-apps
```

To validate the accessToken, you can use a regular expression (regex) to check if the provided key follows any of the Personal Access Token patterns (GH classic or Fine-grain token). You can incorporate the following code snippet into your validation process:

```bash
if [[ "$2" =~ ^(gh[ps]_[a-zA-Z0-9]{36}|github_pat_[a-zA-Z0-9]{22}_[a-zA-Z0-9]{59})$ ]]; then
    echo "Validation successful: DO SOMETHING"
else
    echo "Validation failed: DO SOMETHING"
fi
```

To test accessToken in terminal
```bash
[[ "YOUR GH classic or Fine-grain token" =~ ^(gh[ps]_[a-zA-Z0-9]{36}|github_pat_[a-zA-Z0-9]{22}_[a-zA-Z0-9]{59})$ ]] && echo "ok" || echo "failed"

```


```regex
^(gh[ps]_[a-zA-Z0-9]{36}|github_pat_[a-zA-Z0-9]{22}_[a-zA-Z0-9]{59})$
```

Explanation:

- `^`: Asserts the start of the string.

- `( ... | ...)`: This is a group containing two alternatives separated by `|`. It allows either of the specified patterns.

  - `gh[ps]_[a-zA-Z0-9]{36}`: Matches a string starting with "gh", followed by either 'p' (for Personal Access Tokens) or 's'(for GitHub App server-to-server tokens), an underscore '_', and then exactly 36 alphanumeric characters.

  - `|`: Alternation, indicating that the next part of the regex is an alternative.

  - `github_pat_[a-zA-Z0-9]{22}_[a-zA-Z0-9]{59}`: Matches a string starting with "github_pat_", followed by exactly 22 alphanumeric characters, an underscore '_', and then exactly 59 alphanumeric characters.

- `$`: Asserts the end of the string.

I am writing some doc for AM_modules. I think this will help you a bit.

`draft doc_AM_modules`

To modularize APP-MANAGER, you can follow these steps:

1. **Create a naz.vol.${AM_modules}=`modules` directory**: This directory will contain all the modules. Each module will be a separate script file.

2. **Define a common interface for modules**: Each module should have a function that takes command line arguments and returns a result. The function can access global variables from APP-MANAGER.

    To define a common interface for modules, you can create a function in each module that takes command line arguments and returns a result. This function can access global variables from APP-MANAGER by using the `global` keyword in Bash. 
    
    example:
    ```bash
    # modules/about.am

    function about() {
    # Access global variables from APP-MANAGER
    global APPSPATH

    # Access command line arguments
    local args=("$@")
    echo "Arguments are ${args[@]}"

    # Do something...

    # Return a result
    return 0
    }
    ```


    In this example, `global APPSPATH` allows the `about` function to access the `APPSPATH` global variable from `APP-MANAGER`. The `local args=("$@")` line creates a local array variable `args` that contains all the command line arguments. The `return 0` line returns a result of 0, which indicates success.

    You can create similar functions in other modules. The function name should be the same in all modules, but the function body can be different. This allows you to call the same function in the main script (`APP-MANAGER`) to execute different modules.

    To export a variable from a module to APP-MANAGER, you can use the export keyword in Bash. For example:

    ```bash
    # modules/about.am

    function about() {
    # Export a variable to APP-MANAGER
    export MY_VARIABLE="some value"

    # Rest of the function...
    }
    ```


    In this example, `export MY_VARIABLE="some value"` exports a variable named naz.gen.${gen_var}=`MY_VARIABLE` with the value `"some value"` to the environment. This variable can be accessed by `APP-MANAGER` and any other scripts that are executed after the module.

    Please note that this only exports the variable to scripts that are executed after the module. If you want to export the variable to the current shell (which includes `APP-MANAGER`), you can use the `source` command to execute the module in the current shell. Here's an example:

    ```bash
    source ./modules/about.sh
    ```


    After executing this command, the naz.gen.${gen_var}=`MY_VARIABLE` variable will be available in the current shell.

3. **Modify the main script APP-MANAGER to load and execute modules**: The main script should load the module corresponding to the command line option and execute it.

4. **Pass global variables and command line arguments to modules**: You can pass **global variables** and **command line arguments** to modules as function parameters.

5. **Handle errors and return values carefully**: It's important to handle errors and return values carefully in a modularized Bash script (in fact, in any interpreted language script in general). Here are a few techniques you can use:

   - Use the `set -e` option to exit the script if any command fails. This can help prevent unexpected behavior and potential system damage since AM **runs as root**.
   - Use the `trap` command to handle signals. For example, you can use `trap 'echo "Script interrupted"; exit 1' INT` to exit the script gracefully when it receives an interrupt signal.
   	```bash
   	#!/bin/bash

	# Function to handle cleanup
	cleanup() {
	    echo "Cleaning up before exit..."
	    # Add cleanup tasks here if needed
	    exit 1
	}

	# Set up trap to handle interrupt signal (Ctrl+C)
	trap 'cleanup' INT

	echo "Running script. Press Ctrl+C to interrupt."

	# Simulate a long-running process
	sleep 10

	# This line will only execute if the sleep command completes
	echo " script finished successfully."
	```
   - Use the `exit` command to exit the script with a specific exit code. This can be useful for indicating the success or failure of the script to other programs.
   - Use the `return` command to return a value from a function. This can be useful for passing information back to the main script from a module.

6. **Use the `source` command to execute modules in the current shell**: This allows modules to export variables to the current shell.

Here's a  example of how you can modify the main script to load and execute a module:

```bash
case "$1" in
  '-a'|'about')
    # Load the about module
    source ./modules/about.am
    # Execute the about module
    about "$@"
    ;;
  '-b'|'backup')
    # Load the backup module
    source ./modules/backup.am
    # Execute the backup module
    backup "$@"
    ;;
  # Add more cases for other options...
esac
```
or 

```bash
# APP-MANAGER script

# Import the modules
source modules/backup.am
source modules/clean.am
# ... and so on for other modules

# Call the appropriate module function based on the command line arguments
case "$1" in
    'backup') backup_function "$2" ;;
    'clean') clean_function "$2" ;;
    # ... and so on for other commands
esac
```

And here's an example of how a module might look:

```bash
# modules/about.sh

function about() {
  # Access global variables from APP-MANAGER
  echo "APPSPATH is $APPSPATH"

  # Access command line arguments
  echo "Arguments are $@"

  # Do something...

  # Return a result
  return 0
}
```

### where we are right now?:
- [x] Assess Current Codebase: Analyze the current codebase to identify the most critical areas for modularization.
- [x] Define Modules: Define the scope and responsibilities of each module.
- [ ] Design Interfaces: Design the interfaces between modules to ensure they can work together seamlessly.
- [x] Refactor: Begin refactoring the codebase into modules, starting with the most critical functionalities.
- [ ] Test: Implement comprehensive testing for each module to ensure reliability.
- [ ] Document: Update documentation to reflect the new modular structure.
- [ ] Community Engagement: Encourage community contributions to develop and maintain modules.

My plans and proposal:

I plan to group these 26 modules into some core modules according to the scope and responsibilities of each module so that instead of 26 module imports, we can have 6 or 9!

Initially, we can group them as:

1. **Application Management**: Define the logic for installing, updating, and removing applications into distinct functions and group them.
2. **Dependency Management**: Create a module to handle the installation and management of dependencies required by applications. (Ex. libfuse2)
3. **User Interface**: Abstract the user interface into a separate module to allow for different interfaces (CLI, GUI, etc.).
4. **Configuration Management**: Encapsulate configuration settings and preferences in a dedicated module. (appman config, git_pat config, and so on)
5. **Update Mechanism**: Implement a module to handle updates for both AppImages and other standalone programs.
6. **Sandboxing**: Develop a module for sandboxing applications using tools like Firejail.
7. **Backup and Restore**: Create a module for managing snapshots of applications.
8. **Integration with External Tools**: Modularize the integration with external tools like appimagetool, appimageupdatetool, and pkg2appimage.

For now, these 26 modules are good. We should never ruin user experience, so we can gradually make new core modules like `_app_manage.am` and phase out optional modules like `install.am`, `update.am`, `about.am`. I envision the modules as libraries for the main APP-MANAGER so that it can import a subset of functions that it needs, and not import the whole thing! The modules should be sourced and most of the logic associated with them should remain in the APP-MANAGER; modules should define functions and `main()` if we want to be able to run modules as standalone. I'd add a check at the end of every module if it's being sourced by APP-MANAGER or if it is being run as a script and behave accordingly. (mainly only execute `main()` if it's running as a standalone script and not with an argument as "--source-only $ARGS").

Enough talking, if not today, by tomorrow I'll try to write a core module (POC) and implement source check, function, and error handling, as a guideline for anyone who wants to go ahead with other core modules.

By the way, I'm a BBA final year student, time is pretty tough. I'll add incremental changes as I get time.

Congratulations and thank you for making AM way more readable and manageable than it has ever been. Cheers!

Installing an AppImage from Github is a standard operation, it follows a very specific pattern, so you can be 100% sure that almost all those scripts work.

The only difficulty you may find in writing a script concerns applications not uploaded to github and ZIP/TAR archives. Especially the latter:

- AppImages more or less follow the same installation procedure, and if they are not uploaded to Github, all you have to do is give them a command to intercept the link pointing to the latest version, and this can vary depending on how complex to download the app with `wget` or `curl`. - For TAR/ZIP/7z archives the situation is different, sometimes the author modifies the way of packaging the program and you have to search for it at a lower/greater depth depending on the drug the author was smoking at that moment (see "Mercury" https://github.com/ivan-hc/AM/issues/125).

About patching ~/.profile, this is needed to give ~/.local/bin the right priority in `echo $PATH`

About your suggestion, try to replace 
```
function _patch_bashrc_and_profile(){
	# Check if the custom PATH is not already in .bashrc, then append it (fix - exclamation mark negates the entire command substitution)
	if ! grep -q 'export PATH=$PATH:$(xdg-user-dir USER)/.local/bin' "$HOME/.bashrc"; then
		echo 'export PATH=$(echo $PATH | tr ":" "\n" | grep -v "/.local/bin" | tr "\n" ":" | sed ''s/.$//'')' >> "$HOME/.bashrc"
		echo -e 'export PATH=$PATH:$(xdg-user-dir USER)/.local/bin\n' >> "$HOME/.bashrc"
	fi
	# Correct the order of .local/bin in .profile if necessary
	if grep -q 'PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' "$HOME/.profile"; then
		sed -i 's#PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"#PATH="$PATH:$HOME/.local/bin"#g' "$HOME/.profile"
	fi
}
```
with
```
function _patch_bashrc_and_profile(){
	# Check if the custom PATH is not already in .bashrc, then append it (fix - exclamation mark negates the entire command substitution)
	if ! grep -q 'export PATH=$PATH:$(xdg-user-dir USER)/.local/bin' "$HOME/.bashrc"; then
		echo 'export PATH=$(echo $PATH | tr ":" "\n" | grep -v "/.local/bin" | tr "\n" ":" | sed ''s/.$//'')' >> "$HOME/.bashrc"
		echo -e 'export PATH=$PATH:$(xdg-user-dir USER)/.local/bin\n' >> "$HOME/.bashrc"
	fi
	# Correct the order of .local/bin in .profile if necessary
	if test -f "$HOME/.profile"; then
		if grep -q 'PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' "$HOME/.profile"; then
			sed -i 's#PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"#PATH="$PATH:$HOME/.local/bin"#g' "$HOME/.profile"
		fi
	elif test -f "$HOME/.bash_profile"; then
		if grep -q 'PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' "$HOME/.bash_profile"; then
			sed -i 's#PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"#PATH="$PATH:$HOME/.local/bin"#g' "$HOME/.bash_profile"
		fi
	fi
}
```

This is not a task that other apps other than AppImages can perform easily using a CLI like AM/AppMan:

- The mechanics for an AppImage is "create a directory .home with the same name of the AppImage, near the AppImage";
- Universally its enough to run the app into a dedicated directory to use as a $HOME.

For example, create a new directory
```
mkdir test
cd test
```
then you can run
```
HOME=./
```
or better
```
HOME="$(dirname "$(readlink -f $0)")"
```
from now and for the whole terminal session you can run any app into that directory that will be used as a custom $HOME directory.

If we want to implement such a feature, we should change all the installation scripts for portable apps (non AppImages), add a script that will be symlinked to /usr/local/bin that runs the app into a dedicated directory. This would be an huge work to do.

Easier solution? Push more to convert all the portable apps to the AppImage format. I've done this for many of my apps (see the ones built from .deb or archive, at https://github.com/ivan-hc#my-appimage-packages , fr example Dropbox, Skype, Whatsapp Nativefier, Anydesk...). It was not difficult for some of these, but to convert them in AppImage should not be my task. I'de prefer that the upstream developers take care of this.

The script had a hard coded paths to `~/.local/share`, I changed that so that it checks for $XDG_DATA_HOME instead and sets the '$DATADIR' variable to it, else it sets it to the default path of `$HOME/.local/share`

Defines '$EXECNAME' using the .desktop file in the appimage, it filters the Exec= line to just print the name of the binary that is being run by the appimage, which in 99% of the cases will be the right name. The only issue might be appimages that have multiple Exec= lines in the desktop entry and that might give it the wrong name in that case. 

Finally it makes the symlink to the appimage to `$HOME/.local/bin/$EXECNAME`

I tested it by dropping two appimages at once, one of VLC and another of FIrefox, it correctly placed the .desktop entries in the right directory and also made the symlinks named `vlc` and `firefox` in `$HOME/.local/bin`. Yay!

I did not force exporting the home bin dir to PATH by making the script put command in .bashrc like you suggested before, because of the issues of the login shell being used by the user, not mention that both .bashrc and .zshenv can be in difference locations other than the top level of $HOME.

The XDG Base Dir specification clearly states that it is the distribution that has to make $HOME/.local/bin part of PATH, so I consider the warning is the best approach here tbh, I will leave it to you.

@Samueru-sama also, many Appimages can be updated using "`zsync`", so the upstream developer has nothing to do but update that file without having to change the name to the file.

This is how an AM-updater for .zsync files works, it does not check an upstream version (from an [old template](https://github.com/ivan-hc/AM/blob/main/templates/AM-SAMPLE-for-zsync)):
```
APP=SAMPLE
URL="DIRECTURL2THEAPPIMAGE"

cd /opt/$APP
mkdir tmp
cd ./tmp
wget $URL.zsync 2> /dev/null

cd ..
mv ./tmp/*mage.zsync ./$APP.zsync
rm -R -f ./tmp
zsync /opt/$APP/$APP.zsync
rm -R -f /opt/$APP/*zs-old /opt/$APP/*.part
chmod a+x /opt/$APP/$APP
```

and its for this that newer templates of installation scripts are like this (from new [AM-SAMPLE-AppImage](https://github.com/ivan-hc/AM/blob/main/templates/AM-SAMPLE-AppImage)):
```
APP=SAMPLE
SITE="REPLACETHIS"
version0=$(cat /opt/$APP/version)
version=$(FUNCTION)
if test -f /opt/$APP/*.zsync; then
	mkdir /opt/$APP/tmp
	cd /opt/$APP/tmp
	wget $version.zsync 2> /dev/null
	cd ..
	mv ./tmp/*.zsync ./$APP.zsync
	rm -R -f ./tmp
	zsync /opt/$APP/$APP.zsync
	rm -R -f /opt/$APP/*zs-old /opt/$APP/*.part
	chmod a+x /opt/$APP/$APP
else
	if [ $version = $version0 ]; then
		echo "Update not needed!"
	else
		notify-send "A new version of $APP is available, please wait"
		mkdir /opt/$APP/tmp
		cd /opt/$APP/tmp
		wget $version
		if ls . | grep mage; then
			
			cd ..
			
	  		if test -f ./tmp/*mage; then rm ./version
	  		fi
	  		echo $version >> ./version
	  		mv --backup=t ./tmp/* ./$APP
	  		chmod a+x /opt/$APP/$APP
	  		rm -R -f ./tmp ./*~
		fi
		notify-send "$APP is updated!"
	fi
fi
```

They are called "portable applications" for a reason. They were designed to be downloaded from the author's site and to encourage users to go to the author's site every time to find out about any changes, otherwise they would have been hosted in a centralized repository, such as .deb, .rpm, and .flatpak.. "AM" is just a way to get the latest version without having to open the browser every time... but if you want to get more detailed information about the individual app and what has changed, use the `-a` option and open the link indicated.

Let's not overload the work on this CLI with things that are not our responsibility. I published the https://portable-linux-apps.github.io site to provide a graphical interface, and that's one more thing I did. It shouldn't be my job to open such a site, but that of a community truly interested in growing the work around this CLI, and therefore the publication and management of individual pages. There would need to be a great organization behind all this, but that isn't the case. It's just me, and I also "take care" of the individual app pages (and that's something I really don't want to do).

In this issue, we are talking about adding small details to a CLI that has already gone too far compared to what it should do, from a simple CLI to be used in a Linux terminal, and around which the author (again me) has done too much work to try to make it known to the masses and to encourage them to start a community aimed at keeping Appimages alive as a packaging format, including creating a site and opening 50+ repositories containing 60 different Appimages.

But concretely, what do we have today?

We have to discuss about inserting versions of software packages managed by third parties who don't even know that "AM" exists. And that is. We are nobody. We are just a phantom project, who cares for the few who haven't yet convinced themselves that "Flatpak is the future"!

That said, the option `-a` is sufficient for what you're asking. Really, I don't think there's any point in adding work on things that aren't essential to what "AM" currently is in the Linux world: nothing.

If you've seen such functionality in Synaptics/APT, Pamac/Pacman/YAY and Flatpak/Flathub... good for them, they have such a large and strong community behind them. It's nice to be popular, don't you think?
